abstract.t:
The DAWN working group is defining how a client gets the Minimum Public Discovery Information (MDI) about an AI resource before it interacts with it. The charter covers three settings: a local network, an organization, and cooperating parties over the public Internet.
One proposal for the minimum, the MDI draft, finds that it is the same in all three settings. This document points out that three other things still change with locality: how much a client can learn at or right after discovery, what the client can reasonably assume from where it is looking, and how well it can check who published the information. The last one does not simply get better or worse from local to remote. Records under a party's domain can be validated with DNSSEC, but local multicast advertisements cannot be authenticated, and proxies and catalogs can be authenticated only as themselves.
This is a discussion contribution. It offers some points for the architecture and MDI documents: how local detail relates to the MDI minimum, whether a client should keep track of where a result came from, what to do when local and remote results disagree, and how much weight to give physical proximity as a sign of trust. It proposes no protocol.
